main.title: Soccer
main.summary: Soccer is a soccer video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System.

cards.text: Soccer is a soccer video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo Entertainment System. It was released in Japan and North America in 1985, and in Europe in 1987. An arcade version for the Nintendo VS. System titled VS. Soccer was released the same year. It was released for the Famicom Disk System in 1986. The NES version was released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console on June 12, 2014 and on the Nintendo Classics service in 2018, while the arcade version was released by Hamster Corporation as part of their Arcade Archives series for the Nintendo Switch in 2020.

As with real soccer, the objective is to kick the ball into the opponent's goal. The game features cheerleaders and the option of 15, 30, and 45-minutes halves. Pressing B passes the ball, and A shoots at the opponent's goal.
Seven teams are represented: USA, Great Britain, France, West Germany, Brazil, Japan, and Spain.

When beginning a game, the player chooses whether to play with one or two players. The single-player mode is against the computer with five variable difficulty settings. The player chooses between seven teams and sets a time limit of either 15-, 30-, or 45-minute halves. Games begin in the center of a horizontal field, which pans from side to side with player activity. The player closest to the ball controls it and can kick the ball at the push of a button. An indicator over the closest teammate headed in the same direction as the player indicates who can receive a pass. Goal shots can be controlled with a small meter that represents the ball reaching over the goalie's head. Likewise, the player automatically controls the goalie when the opponent makes a goal shot.

In Japan, Game Machine listed VS. Soccer as the 19th most successful table arcade unit of January 1986. Computer and Video Games said that though every console receives a soccer game, Nintendo's was among the best. They noted the game was somewhat slow and not very attractive, with sparse backgrounds and formless players, but that did not affect the fun. The magazine rated the game 83% overall, with 8/10 for playability and 6/10 for graphics and sound.

main.title: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego?
main.summary: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? is an educational video game released by Broderbund on April 23, 1985.

cards.text: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? is an educational video game released by Broderbund on April 23, 1985. It is the first product in the Carmen Sandiego franchise. The game was distributed with The World Almanac and Book of Facts, published by Pharos Books. An enhanced version of the game was released in 1989, which did not have the almanac-based copy protection and instead used disk-based copy protection. A deluxe version was released in 1990, and features additional animation and a reworked interface from the original version. Some of the bonus features include digitized photos from National Geographic, over 3200 clues, music from the Smithsonian/Folkways Recordings, 20 villains, 60 countries, and 16 maps. CD-ROM versions for MS-DOS and Mac were released in 1992. A Windows version was released in 1994.

In the game, the player takes the role of a rookie in the ACME Detective Agency, tasked to track down crooks from the V.I.L.E. organization who have stolen famous works from around the world. They do this by using their knowledge of geography (aided by the Almanac) to question witnesses or investigate clues to track down where the crook has gone. Successfully solving these crimes increases the player's rank in ACME, leading to more difficult cases and later being tasked with finding the leader of V.I.L.E. and namesake for the game, Carmen Sandiego.

Development began with a menu-driven alternative to the typed commands of adventures such as Colossal Cave Adventure, suited to graphics-capable computers including the Apple II. Adding geography and packaging an Almanac with the game changed its direction. Although initially conceived as an adventure, it proved useful in classrooms and became a successful educational game. By 1995 it had sold more than four million copies and established the Carmen Sandiego franchise. A separate reboot followed in 1996.

main.title: Gradius
main.subtitle: Gradius Turns Power-Ups into Decisions Under Pressure
main.summary: Konami released Gradius in Japanese arcades on May 29, 1985.

cards.heading: Gradius Turns Power-Ups into Decisions Under Pressure
cards.text: Konami released Gradius in Japanese arcades on May 29, 1985. Its Vic Viper flies through horizontally scrolling stages, enemy formations, dangerous terrain and large bosses. Collected capsules advance a cursor along a power-up bar. Players choose when to activate an upgrade, building a combination of speed, missiles, lasers and Options as they survive.

cards.heading: The Capsule Does Not Decide for You
cards.text: Each capsule moves the indicator to the next item on the bar. Activate it and the selected upgrade is gained; collect another capsule and the indicator advances again. Waiting can secure a stronger weapon, but means continuing with the equipment already available. The next section may make an immediate upgrade more useful than the one the player originally intended to save for.

cards.heading: Options Multiply the Ship's Body
cards.text: Options follow the Vic Viper's recent path and fire alongside it. By changing course, players can spread their shots across different parts of the screen. A movement made to avoid an obstacle also changes where those supporting weapons will fire. Positioning the trail becomes part of attacking, especially when enemies approach from several directions.

cards.heading: Dying Means Losing a Construction
cards.text: Losing a life can strip away equipment accumulated across a long run. Reaching a difficult section with a developed ship is very different from restarting there with minimal firepower. Players must learn both the route through a stage and how to recover after a mistake. Protecting the current set of upgrades gives each close escape an immediate value.

main.title: Hang-On
main.summary: Hang-On is a 1985 racing video game developed and published by Sega for arcades.

cards.text: Hang-On is a 1985 racing video game developed and published by Sega for arcades. In the game, the player controls a motorcycle against time and other computer-controlled bikes. It was one of the first arcade games to use 16-bit graphics and uses the Super Scaler arcade system board, created with design input from Yu Suzuki, as technology to simulate 3D effects. The deluxe cabinet version also introduced a motion-controlled arcade cabinet, where the player's body movement on a large motorbike-shaped cabinet corresponds with the player character's movements on screen.

Yu Suzuki began development of Hang-On after deciding to design a motorcycle racing game as a way to use a torsion bar in an arcade game. With market research suggesting GP 500 racing was popular, Suzuki took inspiration from world champion Freddie Spencer and his style of racing. The game's soundtrack was written by Hiroshi Kawaguchi, who used rock music that was uncommon in arcade games at the time. Following its initial release for arcades, Hang-On was ported to Sega's Master System and SG-1000 consoles, as well as to the MSX and PC-88 computers.

Hang-On was very popular at launch and sold well for Sega, becoming the highest-grossing arcade video game of 1985 in the United States and then the highest-grossing arcade game of 1986 in both Japan and the United States. It received a positive critical reception for its realism, graphics, bike cabinet and physical controls, though there was some initial controversy in Japan over modesty concerns involving female players with the bike cabinet. The game started the trend of "taikan" motion simulator games in the late 1980s, which Sega followed with hits such as Space Harrier (1985), Out Run (1986) and After Burner (1987); this helped the arcade video game market recover during the late 1980s. Hang-On has been recognized as a well-remembered and influential arcade game. Several sequels were later made for arcades, as well as video game consoles.

main.title: Gyromite
main.subtitle: Gyromite Places a Physical Robot Inside the Game Loop
main.summary: On August 13, 1985 Nintendo released the Gyro Set for the Family Computer Robot in Japan, associated with the game later known in the West as Gyromite.

cards.heading: Gyromite Places a Physical Robot Inside the Game Loop
cards.text: Nintendo released the Gyro Set for the Family Computer Robot in Japan on August 13, 1985. Its game became known as Gyromite in the West. R.O.B. reads flashing signals from the television, then moves spinning gyros onto an accessory connected to the second controller. Their weight operates gates on screen. The player must coordinate Professor Hector's route with the slower movements of a real robot beside the television.

cards.heading: Six flashing commands move a real robot
cards.text: Powered by four AA batteries housed in its hexagonal base, R.O.B. can rotate its torso left and right along five notched positions, move its arms vertically along a central track, and open and close its hands. Compatible games transmit six distinct commands to the robot—move left, move right, move up, move down, open arms, and close arms—by briefly flashing the television screen at a specific frequency. Both Gyromite and Stack-Up include a "Test" utility mode that sends a continuous optical flash to illuminate the red LED indicator on R.O.B.'s head, confirming that the robot's eyes are properly aligned with the television.

cards.heading: Planning ahead for R.O.B.’s slow movements
cards.text: When Nintendo of America staff unboxed the first shipment of robots from Japan, their initial excitement over the optical technology was tempered by the hardware's sluggish mechanical speed. Howard Phillips recalled that while the wireless light-sensing concept seemed like "voodoo magic", the robot's physical movement was "hysterically slow". Marketing executive Gail Tilden compared demonstrating the unit in person to "watching grass grow", noting that the robot's optical sensors had to be aligned precisely with the television screen to register the flashes. Product designer Don James remarked that playing Gyromite with R.O.B. was challenging because players had to plan two or three moves ahead to accommodate the robot's turning speed, adding that while the device was novel and enjoyable in short bursts, "like Rock 'Em Sock 'Em Robots, I wouldn't want to do it for 40 hours." Tasked with naming the hardware for North America, Tilden initially considered the name "OTTO" as a play on the word "auto" before settling on "Robotic Operating Buddy", or R.O.B.

cards.heading: Spinning gyros hold the gates open
cards.text: The cartridge features three modes: Direct, Game A, and Game B. Direct mode serves as a tutorial that allows the player to send movement commands directly to R.O.B. without playing the main game. In Game A, the player controls Professor Hector with the first controller and presses the Start button to switch control to R.O.B., using the directional pad and the A and B buttons to flash the screen and instruct R.O.B. to pick up a spinning gyro and place it onto the red or blue lever tray. The weight of the spinning gyro holds down the A or B button on the second controller, keeping the corresponding red or blue pillars raised or lowered on screen. In Game B, Professor Hector sleepwalks continuously across 25 stages, and the player controls R.O.B. exclusively without needing to press Start, operating the gates to keep Hector from walking into hazards.

main.title: Ghosts 'n Goblins
main.summary: Ghosts 'n Goblins, known as Makaimura in Japan, is a 1985 platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.

cards.heading: Arthur and the haunted kingdom
cards.text: Ghosts 'n Goblins, known as Makaimura in Japan, is a 1985 platform game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It is the first game in the Ghosts 'n Goblins franchise, and has since been ported to numerous home platforms.

cards.heading: An enduring arcade challenge
cards.text: It was a major commercial success across arcades and home systems. It was among the top ten highest-grossing arcade games of 1986 in Japan and the US, as well as the year's sixth best-selling computer game in the UK, with the Nintendo Entertainment System version selling over 1.6 million units worldwide. It initially received generally positive reviews from critics; it is often cited as one of the most difficult games of all time, and has retrospectively been considered one of the greatest video games ever made.

main.title: Battle City
main.summary: Battle City is a 1985 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for the Family Computer.

cards.text: Battle City is a 1985 multidirectional shooter video game developed and published by Namco for the Family Computer. Released only in Japan, it is the sequel to the arcade video game Tank Battalion.

An arcade version for the Nintendo VS. System, titled VS. Battle City, would follow, along with a Game Boy version in 1991, which was developed and published by Nova Games. The Famicom version was later included as an unlockable in the Japanese release of Star Fox: Assault, and would eventually be digitally re-released via the Virtual Console for Wii and Wii U. Hamster Corporation released the arcade version as part of their Arcade Archives series for the Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 on September 12, 2024.
Although the Famicom version was never officially released outside Japan, Battle City was one of the most common inclusions in unofficial famiclone multicarts.

main.title: Super Mario Bros.
main.subtitle: A World That Teaches as You Move Through It
main.summary: Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka's team built a readable landscape around the pleasure of a jump.

cards.heading: A World That Teaches as You Move Through It
cards.text: Nintendo released Super Mario Bros. for the Famicom in Japan on September 13, 1985. Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka's team built a side-scrolling platform game around running, jumping, power-ups and hidden routes. The first level introduces these actions through its arrangement of enemies, blocks and pipes, allowing a beginner to learn while moving through the world.

cards.heading: The First Level Is a Lesson Without a Classroom
cards.text: World 1-1 took shape late in development and continued to change until the final adjustments. The first Goomba gives players a reason to jump, while blocks overhead reward trying the same action elsewhere. A mushroom emerges from a block, travels right and bounces off a pipe towards Mario. These placements increase the chance that a beginner will discover the power-up while experimenting with the controls.

cards.heading: A Few Pixels Force the Character to Be Readable
cards.text: Mario's early design had to remain readable within a 16-by-16-pixel grid. Miyamoto explained that a hat avoided the problem of animating hair, a moustache defined a face with little room for detail, and contrasting overalls separated the arms from the torso. These practical choices became familiar features of the character. Clear limbs and a recognisable silhouette also helped players follow Mario while running, jumping and changing size.

cards.heading: A Power-Up Teaches Its Value by Moving
cards.text: A Super Mushroom makes Mario larger, lets him survive a hit and changes how he can interact with some blocks. Its movement also helps introduce that advantage. Miyamoto recalled that beginners could mistake it for an enemy. In World 1-1, the pipe sends the mushroom back towards Mario, making an accidental encounter more likely. Collecting it reveals its value immediately through the change in his body.

cards.heading: The Jump Becomes a Measure of Space
cards.text: Mario's jump changes with speed, acceleration and the length of the button press. Before crossing a wide pit, players must judge how much room they have to build speed and where they expect to land. The same platform or enemy can demand a different response when approached at a run. Familiar controls therefore support increasingly precise routes as players learn the movement.

cards.heading: An Obstacle Can Become a Door
cards.text: Green pipes first appear as solid obstacles. Some later become entrances to underground rooms and shortcuts, encouraging players to test a familiar object for another use. Bonus areas and Warp Zones reward this exploration. The main route continues to the right, but a pipe can offer a reason to pause and look for a way elsewhere.

cards.heading: A Grammar Becomes Familiar Across Generations
cards.text: Nintendo identifies Super Mario Bros. as the beginning of the Super Mario series and one of the games that fuelled the Famicom boom. Suspended blocks, transforming power-ups and the flagpole ending became familiar features of its worlds. The same levels accommodate a beginner learning the jump and an experienced player refining a faster route, helping the game sustain repeated play.

cards.heading: Before the landscape came a square
cards.text: The levels began as plans on graph paper. Ground, pipes, enemies and obstacles occupied positions that had to be entered into the program before the team could try them. Moving an object on the drawing produced another playable version to test. The spacing that looked promising on paper could then be judged through the timing of an actual jump.

cards.heading: The music has to know how to run
cards.text: Koji Kondo recalled that an early tune inspired by the sky and greenery failed to match Mario's movement. Running and jumping called for a different rhythm. The score developed in response to that action, accompanying the pace of play as well as the appearance of the scenery.

features.title: Paper, playtests and Mario's team
features.summary: Mario's levels took shape through shared revisions.

cards.heading: A map returns as a playable level
cards.text: Before a Mario level could be tested, somebody had to translate a drawing into data. Toshihiko Nakago recalled receiving graph paper from Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, entering their layouts, then burning a ROM for them to play. Changes returned the following morning. The daily cycle made revision a shared production task rather than a designer's private gesture. A block moved on paper meant another person's work before its new position could be judged with a controller in the player's hands.

cards.heading: Finding a way back from the sky
cards.text: The sky levels nearly disappeared, Nakago recalled, partly because of memory limits. Tezuka proposed reaching them by beanstalk, and Miyamoto made the plant emerge from a struck block. Once there, players could be afraid to jump down. A younger colleague suggested a trail of coins to show the descent. The sequence brought together a destination, an entrance and a visible invitation to return.

cards.heading: Watching somebody else try it
cards.text: Tezuka later described levels that rarely worked as intended on their first attempt. He imagined an enemy arriving at a particular moment, then watched people behave differently. Revision meant responding to those actions, including the tendency to make a course too difficult when its designer already knew every obstacle. His account places testing between an attractive drawing and a finished level. The audience did not merely confirm the team's intention; its unexpected movements supplied information that could change the arrangement itself.

cards.heading: Sound waits for the movement
cards.text: Tezuka recalled supplying his own jumping noises while playing before Kondo's music was ready. The composer joined once the movement was clear enough for him to imagine its sound. Hearing the overworld and underground themes changed how the unfinished game felt to Tezuka. The rhythms the designers had built into movement gave Kondo something to interpret, and his music changed their experience in return.

main.title: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar
main.summary: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, first released in 1985 for the Apple II, is the fourth in the series of Ultima role-playing video games.

cards.heading: An adventure turns towards ethics
cards.text: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, first released in 1985 for the Apple II, is the fourth in the series of Ultima role-playing video games. It is the first in the "Age of Enlightenment" trilogy, shifting the series from the hack and slash, dungeon crawl gameplay of its "Age of Darkness" predecessors towards an ethically nuanced, story-driven approach. Ultima IV has a much larger game world than its predecessors, with an overworld map sixteen times the size of Ultima III and puzzle-filled dungeon rooms to explore. Ultima IV further advances the franchise with dialog improvements, new means of travel and exploration, and world interactivity.

cards.heading: A lasting place in the Ultima series
cards.text: In 1996 Computer Gaming World named Ultima IV as #2 on its Best Games of All Time list for IBM PC compatibles. Designer Richard Garriott considers this game to be among his favorites from the Ultima series.

cards.heading: The next chapter in Ultima
cards.text: Ultima IV was followed by the release of Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny in 1988.

main.title: Space Harrier
main.summary: Space Harrier is a rail shooter developed by Sega and released in 1985 as an arcade video game.

cards.heading: A flight simulator becomes a fantasy
cards.text: Space Harrier is a rail shooter developed by Sega and released in 1985 as an arcade video game. The player navigates surreal landscapes while defeating enemies as a jet-propelled human character. Designed by Yu Suzuki, it was conceived as a realistic military-themed combat flight simulation game, but technical and memory restrictions resulted in Suzuki redesigning it around a fantasy setting. The arcade game is controlled by an analog flight stick while the deluxe arcade cabinet is a cockpit-style linear actuator motion simulator cabinet that pitches and rolls during play, for which it is referred as a taikan or "body sensation" arcade game in Japan.

cards.heading: The appeal of a moving cabinet
cards.text: It was a commercial success in arcades, becoming one of Japan's top two highest-grossing upright/cockpit arcade games of 1986 (along with Sega's Hang-On). Critically praised for its innovative graphics, gameplay and motion cabinet, Space Harrier is often ranked among Suzuki's best works. It has made several crossover appearances in other Sega titles, and inspired a number of clones and imitators, while Capcom and PlatinumGames director Hideki Kamiya cited it as an inspiration for him entering the video game industry.

cards.heading: From arcades to home systems
cards.text: Space Harrier has been ported to over twenty different home computers and home video game consoles. Two home-system sequels followed in Space Harrier 3-D and Space Harrier II (both released in 1988), and the arcade spin-off Planet Harriers (2000). A polygon-based remake of the original game was released by Sega for the PlayStation 2 as part of their Sega Ages series in 2003.
